title: ptgb
description: ptgb is a complete, typed Dart client for the Telegram Bot API: every endpoint, keyboards, media, webhooks, payments, stickers and Business accounts.

Getting Started.Getting Started:
`ptgb` requires Dart SDK `^3.5.0`.

## 1. Install the package

```bash
dart pub add ptgb
```

Or add it to `pubspec.yaml` directly, then run `dart pub get`:

```yaml
dependencies:
  ptgb: ^3.0.0
```

## 2. Write your first bot

```dart
import 'package:ptgb/ptgb.dart';

Future<void> main() async {
  final bot = Bot(); // reads TOKEN from .env, creating a starter file for you

  await for (final update in bot.poll()) {
    if (update.text == '/start') {
      await bot.sendMessage(chatId: update.chatId!, text: 'Hello from ptgb!');
    }
  }
}
```

Every parameter on every `Bot` method (and every constructor in the
library) is named — `chatId: ..., text: ...`, never positional. See
[Configuration](/ptgb/configuration/) for everything the `Bot()`
constructor itself accepts.

## 3. Get a bot token

Run the program above with `dart run bin/my_bot.dart`. The very first
time, since there's no `.env` file next to it yet, `ptgb` creates one for
you and throws an `EnvFileNotFoundException` so you know to fill it in:

```env
# This file holds your bot's secret token. Never share it or commit this
# file to git (add ".env" to your .gitignore).
#
# How to get a token:
#   1. Open Telegram and start a chat with @BotFather.
#   2. Send /newbot and follow the prompts (or /token to reuse an
#      existing bot).
#   3. Copy the token BotFather gives you and paste it below, after the
#      "=" sign, with no spaces and no quotes.
#
# TOKEN=123456789:AAExampleTokenTextGoesRightHere
TOKEN=
```

Open `.env`, follow the instructions inside it, paste your token after
`TOKEN=`, add `.env` to `.gitignore`, and run the program again.

`bot.poll()` is a long-lived `Stream<Update>` — the loop above runs for as
long as your process does. See
[Polling vs. Webhooks](/ptgb/polling-vs-webhooks/) if you'd rather run a
webhook server instead.

## 4. Run it

```bash
dart run bin/my_bot.dart
```

Message your bot on Telegram with `/start` and you should see the reply.

Getting Started.Configuration:
Everything about a `Bot` is configured through its factory constructor:

```dart
factory Bot({
  String? token,
  String dotFileName = '.env',
  String envKey = 'TOKEN',
  String dotEnvTemplate = defaultDotEnvTemplate,
  String? apiBaseUrl,
  String? fileBaseUrl,
  RateLimiter? rateLimiter,
  Duration requestTimeout = const Duration(seconds: 35),
})
```

## Loading the token from a `.env` file (recommended)

```dart
final bot = Bot(); // reads TOKEN from .env, creating a starter file for you
```

The very first time no `.env` file exists next to your script, `ptgb`
writes one for you — populated with `Bot.defaultDotEnvTemplate`, a
beginner-friendly explanation of exactly where to get a token from
[@BotFather](https://t.me/BotFather) and how to paste it in — then throws
an `EnvFileNotFoundException` so you know to open it, fill in the token,
and run your program again:

```env
# This file holds your bot's secret token. Never share it or commit this
# file to git (add ".env" to your .gitignore).
#
# How to get a token:
#   1. Open Telegram and start a chat with @BotFather.
#   2. Send /newbot and follow the prompts (or /token to reuse an
#      existing bot).
#   3. Copy the token BotFather gives you and paste it below, after the
#      "=" sign, with no spaces and no quotes.
#
# TOKEN=123456789:AAExampleTokenTextGoesRightHere
TOKEN=
```

This is handled by the [`penv`](https://pub.dev/packages/penv) package
under the hood. Add `.env` to `.gitignore` so it's never committed.

### Custom file name, key, or starter template

```dart
final bot = Bot(dotFileName: 'secrets.env', envKey: 'BOT_TOKEN');
```

Pass your own `dotEnvTemplate` to change what gets written the first time
`dotFileName` doesn't exist — handy if your bot needs more keys than just
`TOKEN` alongside it:

```dart
final bot = Bot(
  dotEnvTemplate: '''
TOKEN=
DATABASE_URL=
''',
);
```

## Passing the token directly

If you're managing the token yourself — e.g. pulling it from a secrets
manager at deploy time — skip `.env` entirely:

```dart
final bot = Bot(token: myTokenFromSomewhereElse);
```

Never hard-code a real token as a string literal in code that ends up in
version control, either way.

## Pointing at a self-hosted Bot API server

If you run your own
[Telegram Bot API server](https://github.com/tdlib/telegram-bot-api)
instead of using `api.telegram.org`, override the base URLs:

```dart
final bot = Bot(
  token: myToken,
  apiBaseUrl: 'https://my-bot-api.example.com/bot$myToken',
  fileBaseUrl: 'https://my-bot-api.example.com/file/bot$myToken',
);
```

## Automatic rate limiting

Pass a [`RateLimiter`](https://pub.dev/documentation/ptgb/latest/ptgb/RateLimiter-class.html) to have `ptgb` pace outgoing requests for you, instead of handling `429 Too Many Requests` yourself:

```dart
final bot = Bot(
  rateLimiter: RateLimiter(
    globalPerSecond: 30,
    perChatPerMinute: 20,
  ),
);
```

`globalPerSecond` throttles the bot's overall request rate; `perChatPerMinute` throttles requests to any single chat. Both are optional — pass only the one(s) you need, or skip `rateLimiter` entirely to keep the previous (unthrottled) behavior. See `example/17_rate_limiting.dart` for a runnable version.

## Request timeout

`requestTimeout` controls how long a single HTTP call to Telegram is allowed to run before it's aborted, applied on top of the `timeout` seconds you pass to [`poll`](/ptgb/polling-vs-webhooks/#long-polling-botpoll). It defaults to 35 seconds, which already leaves 5 seconds of headroom over `poll`'s default 30-second long-poll timeout:

```dart
final bot = Bot(requestTimeout: const Duration(seconds: 60));
```

If you raise `poll`'s `timeout` parameter, raise `requestTimeout` to match (or exceed it), or every long-poll call will time out before Telegram gets a chance to respond.

## Built-in storage: `BotStorage`

Most bots eventually need to know who has talked to them before. `BotStorage`
gives you file-backed persistence for users and chats — plus any custom data
you attach to them — without setting up a database, powered by
[`pdata`](https://pub.dev/packages/pdata):

```dart
final storage = BotStorage(path: 'bot_data.json');
await storage.load(); // safe even if the file doesn't exist yet

await for (final update in bot.poll()) {
  if (update.from != null) await storage.saveUser(user: update.from!);

  if (update.text == '/users') {
    await bot.sendMessage(
      chatId: update.chatId!,
      text: 'I know ${storage.allUsers().length} user(s) so far!',
    );
  }
}
```

`BotStorage` isn't constructed through `Bot()` — it's a separate class you
create and `load()` once, then call alongside your `Bot`. Every write
(`saveUser`, `saveChat`, `setUserData`, `setChatData`, `removeUser`,
`removeChat`) saves to disk immediately by default; pass
`autoSave: false` and call `save()` yourself to batch writes instead. The
file format (JSON/YAML/TOML) is guessed from `path`'s extension, or set
explicitly via `format`.

Attach your own data to a saved user or chat with `setUserData`/`setChatData`,
and read it back with `getUserData`/`getChatData`:

```dart
await storage.setUserData(userId: user.id, key: 'language', value: 'en');
final language = storage.getUserData(userId: user.id, key: 'language') ?? 'en';
```

See [Bot Storage](/ptgb/examples/42-bot-storage/) for a full runnable
example and the [API Reference](/ptgb/api/bot-storage/) for every method.

## Shutting down

Call `bot.dispose()` when your process is shutting down for good, to
release the underlying HTTP client's resources.

See also: `example/16_custom_env_config.dart` in the package for a
runnable version of the custom-`.env` setup above.
Getting Started.Polling vs Webhooks:
Telegram delivers updates through exactly **one** channel at a time —
`poll()` and `serveWebhook()` are mutually exclusive. Pick one per bot
process.

## Long polling — `Bot.poll()`

Simplest option. No public URL, no TLS certificate, works behind
NAT/localhost. Good default for development and small bots.

```dart
await for (final update in bot.poll()) {
  if (update.text == '/start') {
    await bot.sendMessage(chatId: update.chatId!, text: 'Hi!');
  }
}
```

Internally this repeatedly calls `getUpdates`, so if you've previously
configured a webhook you should call `deleteWebhook()` first — Telegram
won't deliver updates to `getUpdates` while a webhook is active.

## Webhooks — `Bot.serveWebhook()`

Production-style: Telegram pushes updates to an HTTPS URL you control, and
`serveWebhook` runs a local HTTP server to receive them.

Typical flow:

1. Start your server: `await bot.serveWebhook(onUpdate: ..., path: ..., port: ...)`.
2. Register the public URL with Telegram: `await bot.setWebhook(url: ...)`.
3. When you want to go back to polling, call `await bot.deleteWebhook()` first.

```dart
final server = await bot.serveWebhook(
  onUpdate: (update) async {
    final text = update.text;
    final chatId = update.chatId;
    if (text != null && chatId != null) {
      await bot.sendMessage(chatId: chatId, text: 'Received via webhook: $text');
    }
  },
  path: '/telegram-webhook',
  port: 8443,
);

await bot.setWebhook(url: webhookUrl, secretToken: secretToken);
```

Use `getWebhookInfo()` at any time to check what Telegram currently has
registered (URL, pending update count, last error, etc).

## Which should I use?

|  | Polling | Webhook |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Public HTTPS URL required | No | Yes |
| Good for local development | Yes | Needs a tunnel (ngrok, etc) |
| Good for production at scale | Workable, but less efficient | Yes — Telegram pushes only when there's something to deliver |
| Setup complexity | Minimal | Requires `setWebhook` + a reachable server |

## Filtering update types

Both `getUpdates` (used internally by `poll()`) and `setWebhook` accept an
`allowedUpdates` named parameter built from the `UpdateType` enum, so you
only receive the update kinds your bot actually handles (e.g. just
`message` and `callbackQuery`).

## One-time setup

1. Message [@BotFather](https://t.me/BotFather), send `/newbot`, and copy the token.
2. Run any example from the package root:
   ```bash
   dart run example/01_basic_echo_bot.dart
   ```
   The very first time, since there's no `.env` file yet, `ptgb` creates
   one for you with step-by-step instructions inside — open it, paste
   your token after `TOKEN=`, and run the example again. Or create
   `.env` yourself up front:
   ```env
   TOKEN=123456:ABC-your-token-here
   ```

`ptgb_example.dart` passes the token directly (`Bot(token: '...')`) so
it's fully self-contained with no setup — handy to see that this
initialization method exists, but **don't do this in a real project**.
Every other example loads the token from `.env` instead.

## `call`

```dart
Future<dynamic> call(
  String method, [
  Json? params,
  Map<String, InputFile>? files,
]) async {
```

Low-level escape hatch: calls any Telegram Bot API method by name.

uploaded as multipart attachments.

ones made through this method directly — waits its turn first.

## `serveWebhook`

```dart
Future<HttpServer> serveWebhook({
  required void Function(Update update) onUpdate,
  String path = '/',
  Object address = '0.0.0.0',
  int port = 8443,
  SecurityContext? securityContext,
  String? secretToken,
  void Function(Object error, StackTrace stackTrace)? onError,
}) async {
```

Starts an HTTP server that receives Telegram webhook updates and calls
[onUpdate] for each one. Alternative to [poll] for production deployments
behind a reverse proxy or with a direct TLS certificate via [securityContext].
Pair with [setWebhook] so Telegram knows where to send updates.

If parsing the request body or your [onUpdate] callback throws, the
exception is caught (so one bad request can't crash the server) and
passed to [onError] if you provide one — handy for logging. Left
`null` (the default), such errors are swallowed silently, same as
before. Either way, the request still gets an HTTP 200 response, since
Telegram doesn't inspect it.

API Reference.Bot Storage:
*Part of the [API Reference](/ptgb/api-reference/).*

`BotStorage` (from `package:ptgb/ptgb.dart`) is built-in, file-backed
persistence for a bot's users, chats, and any other data you want to
remember between runs — powered by
[`pdata`](https://pub.dev/packages/pdata), so it reads and writes plain
JSON/YAML/TOML files with zero extra dependencies. It's a separate class
from `Bot` — construct one, call `load()` once, and use it alongside your
`Bot` for the lifetime of your program. See
[Configuration](/ptgb/configuration/#built-in-storage-botstorage) for a
narrative walkthrough.

## `BotStorage`

```dart
BotStorage({
  required this.path,
  this.format,
  this.autoSave = true,
})
```

Creates a `BotStorage` backed by the file at `path`. Call `load()` before
reading or writing — this constructor doesn't touch disk.

- `path` — the file this storage reads from and writes to.
- `format` — overrides the format guessed from `path`'s extension. Leave
  `null` to guess from the extension (`.json`, `.yaml`/`.yml`, or `.toml`).
- `autoSave` — whether every mutating call (`saveUser`, `saveChat`,
  `setUserData`, `setChatData`, `removeUser`, `removeChat`) writes to disk
  right away. Set this to `false` and call `save()` yourself if you're
  making many changes at once and want to flush only at the end.

## `load`

```dart
Future<void> load()
```

Reads `path` into memory, creating an empty store if the file doesn't
exist yet. Call this once, right after creating the `BotStorage` and
before your bot starts handling updates.

```dart
final storage = BotStorage(path: 'bot_data.json');
await storage.load();
```

## `save`

```dart
Future<void> save()
```

Writes the current in-memory state to `path`. Called automatically by
every mutating method when `autoSave` is `true` (the default) — you only
need this yourself if you set `autoSave` to `false`.

## `saveUser`

```dart
Future<void> saveUser({required User user})
```

Saves or updates `user` in storage, keyed by their `User.id`. Safe to call
on every incoming update — the first call creates the record, every later
call refreshes their name/username in place.

Any custom data previously set with `setUserData` for this user is
preserved.

```dart
await for (final update in bot.poll()) {
  if (update.from != null) await storage.saveUser(user: update.from!);
}
```

## `saveChat`

```dart
Future<void> saveChat({required Chat chat})
```

Saves or updates `chat` in storage, keyed by their `Chat.id`. Works just
like `saveUser`, but for chats (private chats, groups, supergroups, and
channels).

```dart
await storage.saveChat(chat: update.message!.chat);
```

## `getUser`

```dart
StoredUser? getUser({required int userId})
```

The stored record for the user with the given `userId`, or `null` if that
user has never been saved via `saveUser`.

```dart
final record = storage.getUser(userId: update.userId!);
print(record?.firstName);
```

## `getChat`

```dart
StoredChat? getChat({required int chatId})
```

The stored record for the chat with the given `chatId`, or `null` if that
chat has never been saved via `saveChat`.

## `allUsers`

```dart
List<StoredUser> allUsers()
```

Every user ever saved via `saveUser`, most recently added last.

```dart
for (final user in storage.allUsers()) {
  print('${user.firstName} (${user.id})');
}
```

## `allChats`

```dart
List<StoredChat> allChats()
```

Every chat ever saved via `saveChat`, most recently added last.

## `removeUser`

```dart
Future<bool> removeUser({required int userId})
```

Removes the user with the given `userId` from storage entirely, including
any data set via `setUserData`. Returns `true` if a user was actually

```dart

```

## `setUserData`

```dart
Future<void> setUserData({
  required int userId,
  required String key,
  required dynamic value,
})
```

Stores an arbitrary `value` under `key`, scoped to the user with the given
`userId` — handy for things like a preferred language, a per-user

## `StoredUser`

A read-only view of a user record saved via `BotStorage.saveUser`. You
normally get one of these from `BotStorage.getUser` or
`BotStorage.allUsers` instead of constructing it directly.

| Getter | Type | Description |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `id` | `int` | The user's Telegram ID, matching `User.id`. |
| `isBot` | `bool` | Whether this user is a bot. |
| `firstName` | `String` | The user's first name, as of the last `saveUser` call. |
| `lastName` | `String?` | The user's last name, if set. |
| `username` | `String?` | The user's `@username`, if set. |
| `languageCode` | `String?` | IETF language tag of the user's Telegram client, if known. |
| `data` | `Json` | Any custom data set for this user via `setUserData`. |

## `StoredChat`

A read-only view of a chat record saved via `BotStorage.saveChat`. You
normally get one of these from `BotStorage.getChat` or
`BotStorage.allChats` instead of constructing it directly.

| Getter | Type | Description |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `id` | `int` | The chat's Telegram ID, matching `Chat.id`. |
| `type` | `String` | The chat's type: `'private'`, `'group'`, `'supergroup'`, or `'channel'`. |
| `title` | `String?` | The chat's title, for groups/supergroups/channels. |
| `username` | `String?` | The chat's `@username`, if it has a public one. |
| `firstName` | `String?` | First name of the other party, for private chats. |
| `lastName` | `String?` | Last name of the other party, for private chats. |
| `isPrivate` | `bool` | Whether this is a one-on-one chat with a user. |
| `data` | `Json` | Any custom data set for this chat via `setChatData`. |

Project.FAQ:
### Why do I get "Bad state: No element" or a `TypeError` on the token?

This usually means `.env` wasn't found or doesn't contain the expected
key. As of 3.0.0, if `.env` (or your custom `dotFileName`) doesn't exist
yet, `ptgb` creates a starter one for you and throws an
`EnvFileNotFoundException` instead — open the generated file, paste your
token after `TOKEN=`, and run again. If you're instead seeing this on a
file that already exists, confirm it sits next to `pubspec.yaml` and
contains a `TOKEN=...` line with an actual value, or pass the token
directly: `Bot(token: '...')`. See [Configuration](/ptgb/configuration/).

### I upgraded to 3.0.0 and my code won't compile anymore. What changed?

As of 3.0.0, every parameter on every `Bot` method — and every constructor
in the library (keyboards, media, inline query results, reactions, etc.)
— is named, including previously-positional required ones. So
`bot.sendMessage(chatId, 'hi')` becomes
`bot.sendMessage(chatId: chatId, text: 'hi')`. This is a mechanical,
one-time fix: add the parameter name at each call site the compiler flags.
The [API Reference](/ptgb/api-reference/) shows every method's exact
parameter names. `Bot.call()` is the one exception — it keeps its
low-level `(method, [params, files])` signature since it isn't a typed
wrapper around a specific endpoint.

### Can I use `poll()` and `serveWebhook()` at the same time?

No — Telegram only delivers updates through one channel at a time. Call
`deleteWebhook()` before switching to polling, and `setWebhook()` (not
`poll()`) when running a webhook server. See
[Polling vs. Webhooks](/ptgb/polling-vs-webhooks/).

### Why does `sendMessage` (or similar) throw instead of returning an error object?

Every failed Bot API call throws `TelegramApiException` rather than
returning a nullable/error result — this keeps the happy path free of
null-checks. Catch it where you need to react to failures. See
[Error Handling](/ptgb/error-handling/).

### How do inline query results work now that they're typed?

Each inline result shape (article, photo, gif, video, and so on) has its
own `InlineQueryResult*` class, plus a `Cached*` variant for every media
type that supports a cached `file_id`. Pass a `List<InlineQueryResult>` to
`answerInlineQuery`. See
[Inline Query Result Gallery](/ptgb/examples/41-inline-query-result-gallery/)
for one of every type.

### How do I call a Bot API method that doesn't have a typed wrapper yet?

```dart
await bot.call('someNewMethod', {'param': 'value'});
```

See `Bot.call` in [Core & Session](/ptgb/api/core-session/). This is the
one method in the library that keeps optional positional parameters
rather than named ones, since it's a low-level passthrough rather than a
typed wrapper around a specific endpoint.

### Where do I find every method's exact parameters?

The [API Reference](/ptgb/api-reference/) lists every typed `Bot` method,
grouped by feature area, with its full signature and documentation.

### How do I remember users or chats between runs without a database?

Use the built-in `BotStorage` class — it persists to a plain JSON/YAML/TOML
file via [`pdata`](https://pub.dev/packages/pdata), no database required.
See [Configuration](/ptgb/configuration/#built-in-storage-botstorage),
[Bot Storage](/ptgb/examples/42-bot-storage/), and the
[Bot Storage API Reference](/ptgb/api/bot-storage/).

### What Dart SDK version do I need?

`^3.5.0` or newer, per `pubspec.yaml`.

## 3.0.0

### Breaking

- **Every method on `Bot`, and every constructor across the whole library**
  (keyboards, media, inline query results, message content, permissions,
  stickers, checklists, business/story types) **now takes named parameters
  only.** Positional parameters are gone entirely — including required
  ones:

  ```dart
  // Before (2.x)
  await bot.sendMessage(chatId, 'Hello!');
  InlineKeyboardButton.callback('Yes', 'yes');

  // After (3.0.0)
  await bot.sendMessage(chatId: chatId, text: 'Hello!');
  InlineKeyboardButton.callback(text: 'Yes', data: 'yes');
  ```

  This affects every call site in existing code — the fix is mechanical:
  add the parameter name the compiler asks for. `Bot.call()` is the one

Getting Started.Getting Started:
`ptgb` requires Dart SDK `^3.5.0`.

## 1. Install the package

```bash
dart pub add ptgb
```

Or add it to `pubspec.yaml` directly, then run `dart pub get`:

```yaml
dependencies:
  ptgb: ^2.0.0
```

## 2. Get a bot token

1. Open a chat with [@BotFather](https://t.me/BotFather) on Telegram.
2. Send `/newbot` and follow the prompts.
3. Copy the token it gives you — it looks like `123456:ABC-your-token-here`.
4. Keep it somewhere safe and **never commit it to version control**.

## 3. Load the token

Create a `.env` file next to `pubspec.yaml`:

```env
TOKEN=123456:ABC-your-token-here
```

Add `.env` to `.gitignore`. See [Configuration](/ptgb/configuration/) for
alternatives — passing the token directly, custom file names, and so on.

## 4. Write your first bot

```dart
import 'package:ptgb/ptgb.dart';

Future<void> main() async {
  final bot = Bot(); // reads TOKEN from .env automatically

  await for (final update in bot.poll()) {
    if (update.text == '/start') {
      await bot.sendMessage(update.chatId!, 'Hello from ptgb!');
    }
  }
}
```

`bot.poll()` is a long-lived `Stream<Update>` — the loop above runs for as
long as your process does. See
[Polling vs. Webhooks](/ptgb/polling-vs-webhooks/) if you’d rather run a
webhook server instead.

## 5. Run it

```bash
dart run bin/my_bot.dart
```

Message your bot on Telegram with `/start` and you should see the reply.

## Next steps

- Wrap your handlers in `try`/`catch` before going further — see
  [Error Handling](/ptgb/error-handling/).
- Browse the [Examples](/ptgb/examples/) to add keyboards, media,
  payments, or admin features.
- Look up any method’s exact signature in the
  [API Reference](/ptgb/api-reference/).

```

```

## Automatic rate limiting

Pass a [`RateLimiter`](https://pub.dev/documentation/ptgb/latest/ptgb/RateLimiter-class.html) to have `ptgb` pace outgoing requests for you, instead of handling `429 Too Many Requests` yourself:

```
final bot = Bot(
  rateLimiter: RateLimiter(
    globalPerSecond: 30,
    perChatPerMinute: 20,
  ),
);
```

`globalPerSecond` throttles the bot's overall request rate; `perChatPerMinute` throttles requests to any single chat. Both are optional — pass only the one(s) you need, or skip `rateLimiter` entirely to keep the previous (unthrottled) behavior. See `example/17_rate_limiting.dart` for a runnable version.

## Request timeout

`requestTimeout` controls how long a single HTTP call to Telegram is allowed to run before it's aborted, applied on top of the `timeout` seconds you pass to [`poll`](/ptgb/polling-vs-webhooks/#long-polling-botpoll). It defaults to 35 seconds, which already leaves 5 seconds of headroom over `poll`'s default 30-second long-poll timeout:

```
final bot = Bot(requestTimeout: const Duration(seconds: 60));
```

If you raise `poll`'s `timeout` parameter, raise `requestTimeout` to match (or exceed it), or every long-poll call will time out before Telegram gets a chance to respond.

## Shutting down

Call `bot.dispose()` when your process is shutting down for good, to
release the underlying HTTP client’s resources.

See also: `example/16_custom_env_config.dart` in the package for a
runnable version of the custom-`.env` setup above.
Getting Started.Polling vs Webhooks:
Telegram delivers updates through exactly **one** channel at a time —
`poll()` and `serveWebhook()` are mutually exclusive. Pick one per bot
process.

## Long polling — `Bot.poll()`

Simplest option. No public URL, no TLS certificate, works behind
NAT/localhost. Good default for development and small bots.

```
await for (final update in bot.poll()) {
  if (update.text == '/start') {
    await bot.sendMessage(update.chatId!, 'Hi!');
  }
}
```

Internally this repeatedly calls `getUpdates`, so if you’ve previously
configured a webhook you should call `deleteWebhook` first — Telegram
won’t deliver updates to `getUpdates` while a webhook is active.

## Webhooks — `Bot.serveWebhook()`

Production-style: Telegram pushes updates to an HTTPS URL you control, and
`serveWebhook` runs a local HTTP server to receive them.

Typical flow:

1. Start your server: `await bot.serveWebhook(...)`.
2. Register the public URL with Telegram: `await bot.setWebhook(...)`.
3. When you want to go back to polling, call `await bot.deleteWebhook()` first.

Use `getWebhookInfo()` at any time to check what Telegram currently has
registered (URL, pending update count, last error, etc).

## Which should I use?

|  | Polling | Webhook |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Public HTTPS URL required | No | Yes |
| Good for local development | Yes | Needs a tunnel (ngrok, etc) |
| Good for production at scale | Workable, but less efficient | Yes — Telegram pushes only when there’s something to deliver |
| Setup complexity | Minimal | Requires `setWebhook` + a reachable server |

## Typed helpers & `Update` shortcuts

Every raw field on an `Update` is reachable directly, but two things make working with them more convenient:

**Update shortcuts.** `Update` exposes direct-access getters — `chatId`, `userId`, `text`, `caption`, `messageId`, `messageThreadId`, `replyToMessage`, and more — computed across whichever kind of payload the update actually carries (`message`, `editedMessage`, `channelPost`, callback queries, and so on) via the underlying `anyMessage` fallback. This is what lets the getting-started example write `update.text` and `update.chatId` without first checking which update field is populated. This also covers `subscription` (paired with `UpdateType.subscription`) for changes to a user's Telegram Stars subscription to the bot's content, plus shortcuts for the guest-query and chat-join-request-webapp flows.

**Typed wrappers, everywhere.** As of 2.0.0, `Update`'s payload getters — `callbackQuery`, `inlineQuery`, `chosenInlineResult`, `shippingQuery`, `preCheckoutQuery`, `chatJoinRequest`, `myChatMember`/`chatMember`, `pollAnswer`, `messageReaction`/`messageReactionCount`, `businessConnection`, `deletedBusinessMessages`, `purchasedPaidMedia`, `chatBoost`, `removedChatBoost`, and `subscription` — return their typed wrapper classes (`CallbackQuery`, `InlineQuery`, `ChatMemberUpdated`, `PollAnswer`, ...) directly, instead of raw JSON. The same is true of `Message`'s content getters — `photo`, `location`, `document`, `video`, `audio`, `voice`, `animation`, `videoNote`, `contact`, `venue`, `poll`, `sticker`, `invoice`, `successfulPayment`, `game`, `dice`, `webAppData`, and more — which now hand back `PhotoSize`, `Location`, `Document`, `Video`, and so on rather than a `Json` map. `newChatMembers` is `List<User>` and `leftChatMember` is `User?`.

[`User`](https://pub.dev/documentation/ptgb/latest/ptgb/User-class.html), [`Chat`](https://pub.dev/documentation/ptgb/latest/ptgb/Chat-class.html), [`Message`](https://pub.dev/documentation/ptgb/latest/ptgb/Message-class.html), and every other typed wrapper are thin, read-only, lossless wrappers around the underlying JSON — you can always construct one yourself from a matching `Json` map (`User(someJson)`) if you're working with data that didn't come through a typed getter, and `.raw` stays available on every wrapper underneath for any field not covered by a getter yet.

See `example/18_typed_message_helpers.dart` and `example/19_update_shortcuts_and_any_message.dart` for runnable versions of both.

A minimal reproduction and the relevant Bot API method name help a lot.

Project.FAQ:
### Why do I get “Bad state: No element” or a `TypeError` on the token?

This usually means `.env` wasn’t found or doesn’t contain the expected
key. Confirm the file sits next to `pubspec.yaml` and contains a
`TOKEN=...` line, or pass the token directly: `Bot(token: '...')`. See
[Configuration](/ptgb/configuration/).

### Can I use `poll()` and `serveWebhook()` at the same time?

No — Telegram only delivers updates through one channel at a time. Call
`deleteWebhook()` before switching to polling, and `setWebhook()` (not
`poll()`) when running a webhook server. See
[Polling vs. Webhooks](/ptgb/polling-vs-webhooks/).

### Why does `sendMessage` (or similar) throw instead of returning an error object?

Every failed Bot API call throws `TelegramApiException` rather than
returning a nullable/error result — this keeps the happy path free of
null-checks. Catch it where you need to react to failures. See
[Error Handling](/ptgb/error-handling/).

### How do inline query results work now that they’re typed?

As of 2.0.0, each inline result shape (article, photo, gif, video, and so
on) has its own `InlineQueryResult*` class, plus a `Cached*` variant
for every media type that supports a cached `file_id`. Pass a
`List<InlineQueryResult>` to `answerInlineQuery`. See
[Inline Query Result Gallery](/ptgb/examples/41-inline-query-result-gallery/)
for one of every type.

### How do I call a Bot API method that doesn’t have a typed wrapper yet?

```
await bot.call('someNewMethod', {'param': 'value'});
```

See `Bot.call` in [Core & Session](/ptgb/api/core-session/).

### Where do I find every method’s exact parameters?

The [API Reference](/ptgb/api-reference/) lists every typed `Bot` method,
grouped by feature area, with its full signature and documentation.

### What Dart SDK version do I need?

`^3.5.0` or newer, per `pubspec.yaml`.

Getting Started.Getting Started:
`ptgb` requires Dart SDK `^3.5.0`.

## 1. Install the package

```bash
dart pub add ptgb
```

Or add it to `pubspec.yaml` directly, then run `dart pub get`:

```yaml
dependencies:
  ptgb: ^1.1.0
```

## 2. Get a bot token

1. Open a chat with [@BotFather](https://t.me/BotFather) on Telegram.
2. Send `/newbot` and follow the prompts.
3. Copy the token it gives you — it looks like `123456:ABC-your-token-here`.
4. Keep it somewhere safe and **never commit it to version control**.

## 3. Load the token

Create a `.env` file next to `pubspec.yaml`:

```env
TOKEN=123456:ABC-your-token-here
```

Add `.env` to `.gitignore`. See [Configuration](/ptgb/1.1.1/configuration/) for
alternatives — passing the token directly, custom file names, and so on.

## 4. Write your first bot

```dart
import 'package:ptgb/ptgb.dart';

Future<void> main() async {
  final bot = Bot(); // reads TOKEN from .env automatically

  await for (final update in bot.poll()) {
    if (update.text == '/start') {
      await bot.sendMessage(update.chatId!, 'Hello from ptgb!');
    }
  }
}
```

`bot.poll()` is a long-lived `Stream<Update>` — the loop above runs for as
long as your process does. See
[Polling vs. Webhooks](/ptgb/1.1.1/polling-vs-webhooks/) if you’d rather run a
webhook server instead.

## 5. Run it

```bash
dart run bin/my_bot.dart
```

Message your bot on Telegram with `/start` and you should see the reply.

- Wrap your handlers in `try`/`catch` before going further — see

  payments, or admin features.
- Look up any method’s exact signature in the
  [API Reference](/ptgb/1.1.1/api-reference/).
Getting Started.Configuration:
Everything about a `Bot` is configured through its factory constructor:

```
factory Bot({
  String? token,
  String dotFileName = '.env',
  String envKey = 'TOKEN',
  String? apiBaseUrl,
  String? fileBaseUrl,
  RateLimiter? rateLimiter,
  Duration requestTimeout = const Duration(seconds: 35),
})
```

## Loading the token from a `.env` file (recommended)

```env
TOKEN=123456:ABC-your-token-here
```

```
final bot = Bot(); // reads TOKEN from .env
```

This is handled by the [`penv`](https://pub.dev/packages/penv) package
under the hood. Add `.env` to `.gitignore` so it’s never committed.

### Custom file name or key

```
final bot = Bot(dotFileName: 'secrets.env', envKey: 'BOT_TOKEN');
```

## Passing the token directly

If you’re managing the token yourself — e.g. pulling it from a secrets
manager at deploy time — skip `.env` entirely:

```
final bot = Bot(token: myTokenFromSomewhereElse);
```

Never hard-code a real token as a string literal in code that ends up in
version control, either way.

## Pointing at a self-hosted Bot API server

If you run your own
[Telegram Bot API server](https://github.com/tdlib/telegram-bot-api)
instead of using `api.telegram.org`, override the base URLs:

```
final bot = Bot(
  token: myToken,
  apiBaseUrl: 'https://my-bot-api.example.com/bot$myToken',
  fileBaseUrl: 'https://my-bot-api.example.com/file/bot$myToken',
);
```

## Automatic rate limiting

Pass a [`RateLimiter`](https://pub.dev/documentation/ptgb/latest/ptgb/RateLimiter-class.html) to have `ptgb` pace outgoing requests for you, instead of handling `429 Too Many Requests` yourself:

```
final bot = Bot(
  rateLimiter: RateLimiter(
    globalPerSecond: 30,
    perChatPerMinute: 20,
  ),
);
```

`globalPerSecond` throttles the bot's overall request rate; `perChatPerMinute` throttles requests to any single chat. Both are optional — pass only the one(s) you need, or skip `rateLimiter` entirely to keep the previous (unthrottled) behavior. See `example/17_rate_limiting.dart` for a runnable version.

## Request timeout

`requestTimeout` controls how long a single HTTP call to Telegram is allowed to run before it's aborted, applied on top of the `timeout` seconds you pass to [`poll`](/ptgb/1.1.1/polling-vs-webhooks/#long-polling-botpoll). It defaults to 35 seconds, which already leaves 5 seconds of headroom over `poll`'s default 30-second long-poll timeout:

```
final bot = Bot(requestTimeout: const Duration(seconds: 60));
```

If you raise `poll`'s `timeout` parameter, raise `requestTimeout` to match (or exceed it), or every long-poll call will time out before Telegram gets a chance to respond.

## Shutting down

Call `bot.dispose()` when your process is shutting down for good, to
release the underlying HTTP client’s resources.

See also: `example/16_custom_env_config.dart` in the package for a
runnable version of the custom-`.env` setup above.
Getting Started.Polling vs Webhooks:
Telegram delivers updates through exactly **one** channel at a time —
`poll()` and `serveWebhook()` are mutually exclusive. Pick one per bot
process.

## Long polling — `Bot.poll()`

Simplest option. No public URL, no TLS certificate, works behind
NAT/localhost. Good default for development and small bots.

```
await for (final update in bot.poll()) {
  if (update.text == '/start') {
    await bot.sendMessage(update.chatId!, 'Hi!');
  }
}
```

Internally this repeatedly calls `getUpdates`, so if you’ve previously
configured a webhook you should call `deleteWebhook` first — Telegram
won’t deliver updates to `getUpdates` while a webhook is active.

## Webhooks — `Bot.serveWebhook()`

Production-style: Telegram pushes updates to an HTTPS URL you control, and
`serveWebhook` runs a local HTTP server to receive them.

Typical flow:

1. Start your server: `await bot.serveWebhook(...)`.
2. Register the public URL with Telegram: `await bot.setWebhook(...)`.
3. When you want to go back to polling, call `await bot.deleteWebhook()` first.

Use `getWebhookInfo()` at any time to check what Telegram currently has
registered (URL, pending update count, last error, etc).

## Which should I use?

|  | Polling | Webhook |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Public HTTPS URL required | No | Yes |
| Good for local development | Yes | Needs a tunnel (ngrok, etc) |
| Good for production at scale | Workable, but less efficient | Yes — Telegram pushes only when there’s something to deliver |
| Setup complexity | Minimal | Requires `setWebhook` + a reachable server |

Both `getUpdates` (used internally by `poll()`) and `setWebhook` accept an

and `callbackQuery`).

## Typed helpers & `Update` shortcuts

Every raw field on an `Update` is reachable directly, but two things make working with them more convenient:

**Update shortcuts.** `Update` exposes direct-access getters — `chatId`, `userId`, `text`, `caption`, `messageId`, `messageThreadId`, `replyToMessage`, and more — computed across whichever kind of payload the update actually carries (`message`, `editedMessage`, `channelPost`, callback queries, and so on) via the underlying `anyMessage` fallback. This is what lets the getting-started example write `update.text` and `update.chatId` without first checking which update field is populated. As of 1.1.0 this also covers `subscription` (paired with `UpdateType.subscription`) for changes to a user's Telegram Stars subscription to the bot's content, plus shortcuts for the new guest-query and chat-join-request-webapp flows.

**Typed wrappers.** [`User`](https://pub.dev/documentation/ptgb/latest/ptgb/User-class.html), [`Chat`](https://pub.dev/documentation/ptgb/latest/ptgb/Chat-class.html), and [`Message`](https://pub.dev/documentation/ptgb/latest/ptgb/Message-class.html) are thin, read-only, lossless wrappers around the raw JSON `Update` already hands you — construct one from any matching `Json` you have (`User(update.from!)`) to get typed getters (`id`, `firstName`, `isPremium`, ...) instead of manual `as` casts, with the original `raw` map always available underneath for anything not covered by a getter. Wrapping is entirely optional; the raw-JSON style shown throughout this reference still works exactly as before.

See `example/18_typed_message_helpers.dart` and `example/19_update_shortcuts_and_any_message.dart` for runnable versions of both.

Bug reports, feature requests, and pull requests are welcome on

## Filing a bug

A minimal reproduction and the relevant Bot API method name help a lot.
Please include:

- The `ptgb` version you’re using.
- The Dart SDK version (`dart --version`).
- The method(s) involved, and the exact `TelegramApiException` (if any) —
  see [Error Handling](/ptgb/1.1.1/error-handling/).
- A minimal code snippet that reproduces the issue.

## Requesting a feature

If the Bot API added a new method or field that `ptgb` doesn’t wrap yet,
note the method name from the
[official Bot API docs](https://core.telegram.org/bots/api) — new
endpoints can also be reached immediately through the low-level
`Bot.call()` escape hatch while a typed wrapper is added.

## Pull requests

- Keep changes focused; separate unrelated fixes into separate PRs.
- Match the existing style: typed methods return `Json`/`List<Json>`/`bool`
  wrappers around `Bot.call`, with full `///` doc comments.
- Add or update an example in `example/` if you’re introducing
  user-facing behavior.
- Run `dart analyze` and `dart format` before submitting.

Project.FAQ:
### Why do I get “Bad state: No element” or a `TypeError` on the token?

This usually means `.env` wasn’t found or doesn’t contain the expected
key. Confirm the file sits next to `pubspec.yaml` and contains a
`TOKEN=...` line, or pass the token directly: `Bot(token: '...')`. See
[Configuration](/ptgb/1.1.1/configuration/).

### Can I use `poll()` and `serveWebhook()` at the same time?

No — Telegram only delivers updates through one channel at a time. Call
`deleteWebhook()` before switching to polling, and `setWebhook()` (not
`poll()`) when running a webhook server. See
[Polling vs. Webhooks](/ptgb/1.1.1/polling-vs-webhooks/).

### Why does `sendMessage` (or similar) throw instead of returning an error object?

Every failed Bot API call throws `TelegramApiException` rather than
returning a nullable/error result — this keeps the happy path free of
null-checks. Catch it where you need to react to failures. See
[Error Handling](/ptgb/1.1.1/error-handling/).

### Why are inline query results raw `Map`s instead of typed classes?

There are many inline result types (article, photo, gif, video, and more)
with very different shapes, so typing all of them individually isn’t
currently worth the API surface — this is intentional for now.

### How do I call a Bot API method that doesn’t have a typed wrapper yet?

```
await bot.call('someNewMethod', {'param': 'value'});
```

See `Bot.call` in [Core & Session](/ptgb/1.1.1/api/core-session/).

### Where do I find every method’s exact parameters?

The [API Reference](/ptgb/1.1.1/api-reference/) lists every typed `Bot` method,
grouped by feature area, with its full signature and documentation.

### What Dart SDK version do I need?

`^3.5.0` or newer, per `pubspec.yaml`.

`ptgb` requires Dart SDK `^3.5.0`.

## 1. Install the package

```bash
dart pub add ptgb
```

Or add it to `pubspec.yaml` directly, then run `dart pub get`:

```yaml
dependencies:
  ptgb: ^1.0.0
```

## 2. Get a bot token

1. Open a chat with [@BotFather](https://t.me/BotFather) on Telegram.
2. Send `/newbot` and follow the prompts.
3. Copy the token it gives you — it looks like `123456:ABC-your-token-here`.
4. Keep it somewhere safe and **never commit it to version control**.

## 3. Load the token

Create a `.env` file next to `pubspec.yaml`:

```env
TOKEN=123456:ABC-your-token-here
```

Add `.env` to `.gitignore`. See [Configuration](/ptgb/1.0.0/configuration/) for
alternatives — passing the token directly, custom file names, and so on.

## 4. Write your first bot

```dart
import 'package:ptgb/ptgb.dart';

Future<void> main() async {
  final bot = Bot(); // reads TOKEN from .env automatically

  await for (final update in bot.poll()) {
    if (update.text == '/start') {
      await bot.sendMessage(update.chatId!, 'Hello from ptgb!');
    }
  }
}
```

`bot.poll()` is a long-lived `Stream<Update>` — the loop above runs for as
long as your process does. See
[Polling vs. Webhooks](/ptgb/1.0.0/polling-vs-webhooks/) if you’d rather run a
webhook server instead.

## 5. Run it

```bash
dart run bin/my_bot.dart
```

Message your bot on Telegram with `/start` and you should see the reply.

Everything about a `Bot` is configured through its factory constructor:

```
factory Bot({
  String? token,
  String dotFileName = '.env',
  String envKey = 'TOKEN',
  String? apiBaseUrl,
  String? fileBaseUrl,
})
```

## Loading the token from a `.env` file (recommended)

```env
TOKEN=123456:ABC-your-token-here
```

```
final bot = Bot(); // reads TOKEN from .env
```

This is handled by the [`penv`](https://pub.dev/packages/penv) package
under the hood. Add `.env` to `.gitignore` so it’s never committed.

### Custom file name or key

```
final bot = Bot(dotFileName: 'secrets.env', envKey: 'BOT_TOKEN');
```

## Passing the token directly

If you’re managing the token yourself — e.g. pulling it from a secrets
manager at deploy time — skip `.env` entirely:

```
final bot = Bot(token: myTokenFromSomewhereElse);
```

Never hard-code a real token as a string literal in code that ends up in
version control, either way.

## Pointing at a self-hosted Bot API server

If you run your own
[Telegram Bot API server](https://github.com/tdlib/telegram-bot-api)
instead of using `api.telegram.org`, override the base URLs:

```
final bot = Bot(
  token: myToken,
  apiBaseUrl: 'https://my-bot-api.example.com/bot$myToken',
  fileBaseUrl: 'https://my-bot-api.example.com/file/bot$myToken',
);
```

## Shutting down

Call `bot.dispose()` when your process is shutting down for good, to
release the underlying HTTP client’s resources.

See also: `example/16_custom_env_config.dart` in the package for a
runnable version of the custom-`.env` setup above.
Getting Started.Polling vs Webhooks:
**You are viewing the archived v1.0.0 docs.** [Go to the latest version (v1.1.0) →](/ptgb/polling-vs-webhooks/)

Telegram delivers updates through exactly **one** channel at a time —
`poll()` and `serveWebhook()` are mutually exclusive. Pick one per bot
process.

## Long polling — `Bot.poll()`

Simplest option. No public URL, no TLS certificate, works behind
NAT/localhost. Good default for development and small bots.

```
await for (final update in bot.poll()) {
  if (update.text == '/start') {
    await bot.sendMessage(update.chatId!, 'Hi!');
  }
}
```

Internally this repeatedly calls `getUpdates`, so if you’ve previously
configured a webhook you should call `deleteWebhook` first — Telegram
won’t deliver updates to `getUpdates` while a webhook is active.

## Webhooks — `Bot.serveWebhook()`

Production-style: Telegram pushes updates to an HTTPS URL you control, and
`serveWebhook` runs a local HTTP server to receive them.

Typical flow:

1. Start your server: `await bot.serveWebhook(...)`.
2. Register the public URL with Telegram: `await bot.setWebhook(...)`.
3. When you want to go back to polling, call `await bot.deleteWebhook()` first.

Use `getWebhookInfo()` at any time to check what Telegram currently has
registered (URL, pending update count, last error, etc).

## Which should I use?

|  | Polling | Webhook |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Public HTTPS URL required | No | Yes |
| Good for local development | Yes | Needs a tunnel (ngrok, etc) |
| Good for production at scale | Workable, but less efficient | Yes — Telegram pushes only when there’s something to deliver |
| Setup complexity | Minimal | Requires `setWebhook` + a reachable server |

See `example/10_webhook_server.dart` for a full runnable webhook setup,

## Filtering update types

Both `getUpdates` (used internally by `poll()`) and `setWebhook` accept an
`allowedUpdates` list built from the `UpdateType` enum, so you only
receive the update kinds your bot actually handles (e.g. just `message`
and `callbackQuery`).

## `call`

```dart
Future<dynamic> call(String method, [Json? params, Map<String, InputFile>? files]) =>
```

Low-level escape hatch: calls any Telegram Bot API method by name.

Use this for brand-new API methods that don’t have a typed wrapper yet.
[method] is the raw Bot API method name (e.g. `'sendMessage'`), [params]
is the JSON body, and [files] are any [InputFile]s that should be
uploaded as multipart attachments.

```dart

```

## `logOut`

```dart

```

Logs the bot out from the Bot API server before moving it to a local server instance.
You generally never need this unless you’re running your own Bot API server.

## `close`

```dart

```

Closes the bot instance before moving it from one local server to another.
Not related to [dispose] — this is a Telegram API call, not local cleanup.

Project.Contributing:

Bug reports, feature requests, and pull requests are welcome on
[GitHub](https://github.com/psdkjoon/ptgb).

## Filing a bug

A minimal reproduction and the relevant Bot API method name help a lot.
Please include:

- The `ptgb` version you’re using.
- The Dart SDK version (`dart --version`).
- The method(s) involved, and the exact `TelegramApiException` (if any) —
  see [Error Handling](/ptgb/1.0.0/error-handling/).
- A minimal code snippet that reproduces the issue.

## Requesting a feature

If the Bot API added a new method or field that `ptgb` doesn’t wrap yet,
note the method name from the
[official Bot API docs](https://core.telegram.org/bots/api) — new
endpoints can also be reached immediately through the low-level
`Bot.call()` escape hatch while a typed wrapper is added.

## Pull requests

- Keep changes focused; separate unrelated fixes into separate PRs.
- Match the existing style: typed methods return `Json`/`List<Json>`/`bool`
  wrappers around `Bot.call`, with full `///` doc comments.
- Add or update an example in `example/` if you’re introducing
  user-facing behavior.
- Run `dart analyze` and `dart format` before submitting.

### Why do I get “Bad state: No element” or a `TypeError` on the token?

This usually means `.env` wasn’t found or doesn’t contain the expected
key. Confirm the file sits next to `pubspec.yaml` and contains a
`TOKEN=...` line, or pass the token directly: `Bot(token: '...')`. See
[Configuration](/ptgb/1.0.0/configuration/).

### Can I use `poll()` and `serveWebhook()` at the same time?

No — Telegram only delivers updates through one channel at a time. Call
`deleteWebhook()` before switching to polling, and `setWebhook()` (not
`poll()`) when running a webhook server. See
[Polling vs. Webhooks](/ptgb/1.0.0/polling-vs-webhooks/).

### Why does `sendMessage` (or similar) throw instead of returning an error object?

Every failed Bot API call throws `TelegramApiException` rather than
returning a nullable/error result — this keeps the happy path free of
null-checks. Catch it where you need to react to failures. See
[Error Handling](/ptgb/1.0.0/error-handling/).

### Why are inline query results raw `Map`s instead of typed classes?

There are many inline result types (article, photo, gif, video, and more)
with very different shapes, so typing all of them individually isn’t
currently worth the API surface — this is intentional for now.

### How do I call a Bot API method that doesn’t have a typed wrapper yet?

```
await bot.call('someNewMethod', {'param': 'value'});
```

See `Bot.call` in [Core & Session](/ptgb/1.0.0/api/core-session/).

### Where do I find every method’s exact parameters?

The [API Reference](/ptgb/1.0.0/api-reference/) lists every typed `Bot` method,
grouped by feature area, with its full signature and documentation.

### What Dart SDK version do I need?

`^3.5.0` or newer, per `pubspec.yaml`.
